AcceptInvitationRequest.description:
Redeem a seat invitation and choose a password — Epic 9.14.

`full_name` is required here and not on the invitation itself: the person
who sent the invite knows an email address, not how the recipient writes
their own name. Until this is submitted the seat list shows the address,
which is the only fact anybody has.
AcceptInvitationRequest.title: AcceptInvitationRequest

ActionItemListOut.description: The scan's fix list, plus what happened the last time it was generated.
ActionItemListOut.title: ActionItemListOut

ActionItemOut.description: One generated fix — §5.3's prioritised action list.
ActionItemOut.title: ActionItemOut

ActionItemSource.description:
Which Epic 7 candidate produced this fix.

Deliberately only two members. An LLM-authored fix is not a third source —
it is the same measured gap or audit finding, worded better, and modelling
it as its own source would let a generated recommendation exist without a
measurement behind it.
ActionItemSource.title: ActionItemSource

AlertOut.description: One detected change, with both scans it sits between.
AlertOut.title: AlertOut

AnswerGapBrandOut.description: One column of the grid: a brand, and how much of this scan it won.
AnswerGapBrandOut.title: AnswerGapBrandOut

AnswerGapCellOut.description:
One cell: how many of this prompt's engines named this brand.

`named_on` is a count and not a boolean because the engines disagree, and
that disagreement is the finding — a rival named by one engine of three is
a different competitive position from one named by all three.
AnswerGapCellOut.title: AnswerGapCellOut

AnswerGapRivalOut.description:
A rival, counted across the client's WHOLE history.

The cross-scan half of "how often does this recur". Competitors persist
between scans where prompts do not, so this is the only axis on which a
recurring gap can honestly be counted over time.
AnswerGapRivalOut.title: AnswerGapRivalOut

AnswerGapRowOut.description: One prompt, across every engine that answered it.
AnswerGapRowOut.title: AnswerGapRowOut

AnswerGapsOut.description: The Answer gaps read for one scan, plus the cross-scan rival rollup.
AnswerGapsOut.title: AnswerGapsOut

AuditCheckOut.description: One check's verdict — §7's "pass/fail + detail for each check".
AuditCheckOut.title: AuditCheckOut

AuditStatus.description:
Outcome of an audit run.

Added in Epic 6. Without it a failed crawl and a genuinely bare site are
indistinguishable — both would be a row of nulls — and the Technical
Foundation sub-score must never treat "we could not read the site" as
"the site has no markup". Same discipline as ClassificationStatus,
DetectionStatus and ScoreStatus.
AuditStatus.title: AuditStatus

AutoRescanOut.description:
A client's monthly-rescan setting, as the caller may see it.

`available` is true only when the API has automatic rescans on (`AUTO_RESCAN_ENABLED`) AND the
caller is an owner or admin. When it is false everything else is its empty value, whatever
the client holds, and the web draws nothing. `skipReason` is one of our own codes
(`AGENCY_NOT_PAID`, `ALLOWANCE_USED`, `USER_NOT_ADMIN`, `COULD_NOT_START`) or null; with it,
`skippedAt` is when the last attempt started no scan and `retriesAt` is the first instant of
the next UTC calendar month, when it is tried again.
AutoRescanOut.title: AutoRescanOut

BillingPlanOut.description:
What the plan offers the public — today, only the length of its free trial.

`GET /billing/plan`, with no session, no agency and nothing secret in it:
it is read by the public pricing card and landing page, before anybody has
signed up. `trialDays` is `STRIPE_TRIAL_DAYS`, the one place the length of
the trial is stated, so what a page says and what checkout does cannot
disagree. **0 means there is no trial**, and is also the answer on a
deployment where checkout is not configured (a trial nobody can start is
not one to promise). A page says "the first N days after you subscribe are
free" only for an N above 0.

It describes the offer to a NEW agency. Whether a particular agency still
gets the trial is not here: that is the agency's own history, and checkout
decides it (`services/billing.create_checkout_session`).
BillingPlanOut.title: BillingPlanOut

BillingStatusOut.description:
An agency's subscription, as recorded — never as freshly asked of Stripe.

Every field here is read from the `agencies` row. **This endpoint makes no
call to Stripe**, which is a deliberate property rather than an optimisation:
a settings screen that reached a payment API on every page load would be
slower, would fail when Stripe was slow, and would put a third party in the
path of a page that has four other things to render. The webhook is what
keeps these columns true.

`subscriptionStatus` is Stripe's own string, passed through unmapped — see
`models/tenancy.py` for why the column is not an enum. A client that wants
to know "is this agency paid up" should read `isActive` rather than
comparing strings, because the set of statuses that mean yes is a decision
that lives in `services/billing.py` and may grow.
BillingStatusOut.title: BillingStatusOut

BrandingOut.description: An agency's branding as stored. Null on both fields is unbranded.
BrandingOut.title: BrandingOut

BrandingRequest.description:
What an agency may change about how its reports look — Epic 9.22.

**The shortness of this model is the decision, not an omission.** §7 line 2
asked for "logo, custom domain, colours"; what an agency may actually
change is a logo and ONE colour used only on chrome.

The report's palette is notation. `--avp-vis-*` encodes the score on a
monotonic lightness ramp that survives greyscale and colour-vision
deficiency; `--avp-competitor-{1..5}` is neutral so no rival reads as
endorsed or attacked; `--avp-beacon-*` marks the subject being scanned, who
is the prospect and not the agency; the semantic four say a scan failed or
a quota is low. There is no field here that can reach any of them, which is
the guarantee — enforced by the type rather than by a reviewer noticing,
the same way `FixFacts` has no field able to hold page copy.

**No `custom_domain`.** Deferred rather than forgotten: it needs DNS
verification, certificate issuance and routing before it does anything, and
a field that stores a value nothing honours is a field that looks built.

**Both values are explicitly nullable, and null means "remove it".** An
agency that uploaded the wrong logo needs a way back to unbranded, and a
PATCH that can only ever set is a one-way door.
BrandingRequest.title: BrandingRequest

ChangePasswordRequest.description:
Change your own password while signed in — Epic 9.14.

`current_password` is presented, not set, so it carries the login bounds
for the reason `LoginRequest` gives. `new_password` is set, so it carries
the full rule — the same `Password` sign-up and reset-confirm use.
ChangePasswordRequest.title: ChangePasswordRequest

CheckoutSessionOut.description:
Where to send the browser to pay.

A URL and nothing else. The frontend navigates to it; there is no Stripe
JavaScript library in `apps/web` and this shape is why one is not needed.
CheckoutSessionOut.title: CheckoutSessionOut

CitedDomainOut.description:
A domain an engine cited, and how often.

Domain + URL + count. api-contracts.md and the facts-only rule both permit
cited domains and URLs explicitly; the cited PAGE's text is never read,
stored, or shown. `sample_url` is a link out to the source — the sanctioned
alternative to quoting it.
CitedDomainOut.title: CitedDomainOut

ClassificationStatus.description:
Outcome of Epic 2's industry classification.

Deliberately mirrors Score.status (scoring-spec.md): a result we could not
determine is recorded as such, never as a confident-looking guess.
ClassificationStatus.title: ClassificationStatus

ClientDetailOut.description: A client plus the crawl facts from its most recent classification.
ClientDetailOut.title: ClientDetailOut

ClientHistoryOut.description: Every scan of one client that produced a reading, oldest first.
ClientHistoryOut.title: ClientHistoryOut

ClientKind.description:
A prospect becomes a client when the deal closes.

The same row transitions rather than being recreated, so the scan history
gathered while prospecting becomes the "before" half of the before/after
ROI report in Epic 11.
ClientKind.title: ClientKind

CompetitorInput.description: One competitor in an operator's replacement set.
CompetitorInput.title: CompetitorInput

CompetitorScoreOut.description:
Per-competitor figures for the three measurable dimensions.

**There is deliberately no `composite`.** Sentiment is classified toward the
subject only (Epic 4.3) and Technical Foundation arrives in Epic 6, so 25%
of the weight has no per-competitor input. A composite computed over a
different weight basis would not be comparable to the subject's, which is
the entire purpose of a comparison.
CompetitorScoreOut.title: CompetitorScoreOut

CompleteGoogleSignUpRequest.description:
Finish creating an agency after Google has verified the person — Epic 20.

The same two facts `SignUpRequest` asks for that Google cannot supply: what
the agency is called, and how the person writes their own name (Google's
`name` is a suggestion, not an answer). No email — it is the ticket's — and
no password, which is the point.
CompleteGoogleSignUpRequest.title: CompleteGoogleSignUpRequest

ConfirmedSiteOut.description: A domain the agency confirmed as a brand's own other site.
ConfirmedSiteOut.title: ConfirmedSiteOut

CrawlSummaryOut.description: FACTS from the crawl. Never page content — see services/crawl.py.
CrawlSummaryOut.title: CrawlSummaryOut

CrawlerAccessOut.description: The AI crawler access policy read during one scan's technical audit.
CrawlerAccessOut.title: CrawlerAccessOut

CrawlerAccessSummaryOut.description:
Counts across the roster, for the screen's stat row.

`searchBlocked` is separated from `blocked` because it is the finding with
a cost attached. Blocking a TRAINING crawler is a rights decision that
costs no citations. Blocking a SEARCH crawler removes the site from the
retrieval index an engine cites from — which is this product's whole
subject — and an agency that blanket-blocked "AI bots" to protect its
content has usually bought that by accident.
CrawlerAccessSummaryOut.title: CrawlerAccessSummaryOut

CrawlerAgentOut.description: One AI crawler's verdict for one scan.
CrawlerAgentOut.title: CrawlerAgentOut

CreateClientRequest.description:
Intake payload.

`url` is intentionally permissive — an operator pastes whatever they have,
including a bare domain. Normalisation and validation happen server-side in
services/intake.py:parse_domain so the browser and the API cannot disagree
about what counts as a valid address.
CreateClientRequest.title: CreateClientRequest

CrossEngineOut.description:
Where the engines agree and where they do not — Epic 9.23, Layer 3.

**`agreementRate` is null when nothing was comparable, and that is not
100%.** A scan where only one engine answered agrees with itself trivially;
reporting it as perfect consensus would make the strongest available claim
from the weakest available evidence. `comparablePrompts` is the denominator
every figure here is honest about.

**`standings` is `[]` for a scan whose status is `failed`** (checklist 3.37,
extending 3.24 and 3.30). A standing's mention rate and sentiment are
computed by the scoring functions, and the sentiments add up to the
Sentiment sub-score, which a failed scan does not show. `splits`,
`comparablePrompts` and `agreementRate` are facts about which engines named
the subject and are served as for any other status.
CrossEngineOut.title: CrossEngineOut

CurrentQuestionSetOut.description:
The set a rescan of this client would copy, and where it came from.

`source_scan_id` and `written_at` are the scan that wrote it; `reused_since` is the date of the
first scan that copied it (null while none has). `written_with_rivals` is the rival names the
questions were written with (null for a set written before they were recorded) and
`rivals_changed` is true when the client's current active rivals differ from them (false when
they are not known).
CurrentQuestionSetOut.title: CurrentQuestionSetOut

DetectionStatus.description:
Outcome of a competitor-detection run.

Mirrors ClassificationStatus and Score's INSUFFICIENT_DATA: a detection we
could not make confidently must be representable as such, rather than
surfacing a thin or contradictory set as though it were a finding.
DetectionStatus.title: DetectionStatus

Engine.description: AI answer engines. §7 Epic 4 starts with two, behind a common interface.
Engine.title: Engine

EngineCoverageOut.description: How one engine covered the prompt set. Counts only.
EngineCoverageOut.title: EngineCoverageOut

EngineStandingOut.description:
One engine's own view of the subject — Epic 9.23.

The same two axes the composite is built from, computed by the same
functions on that engine's slice of the results. `sentiment` is null when
this engine never named the subject: no mention means no sentiment, the
same exclusion scoring makes for the scan as a whole rather than scoring
an absence zero twice.
EngineStandingOut.title: EngineStandingOut

GapKind.description:
One prompt's verdict for this client. Ordered by how bad it is.

Precedence when several could apply is the declaration order below, worst
first — a prompt that is both absent AND uncited is reported as `absent`,
because being named at all comes before being cited.
GapKind.title: GapKind

GooglePendingOut.description:
What Google told us about a person who has no account yet — Epic 20.

Read by the sign-up completion page so it can show the address the
account will be under and pre-fill the name. Nothing here is a credential;
the ticket is.
GooglePendingOut.title: GooglePendingOut

GooglePendingRequest.description: The ticket to peek at, in a body so it never lands in a URL.
GooglePendingRequest.title: GooglePendingRequest

HistoryCitedDomainOut.description:
One domain and how often this scan's answers cited it.

Not the report's `CitedDomainOut`. That one carries a `sample_url` and is
ranked and TRUNCATED for display; this is the full per-scan tally a trend
needs, so borrowing that shape would mean inheriting a display cap into a
time series.
HistoryCitedDomainOut.title: HistoryCitedDomainOut

HistoryCompetitorOut.description:
One rival's comparable figures for one scan.

No composite, for the reason `ReportCompetitorOut` gives at length:
sentiment is classified toward the subject only and technical foundation is
the subject's own site, so 25% of the weight has no per-competitor input and
a rival "composite" would not be comparable to the subject's.
HistoryCompetitorOut.title: HistoryCompetitorOut

HistoryQuestionSetOut.description: Which questions a scan asked — F6. Ids and a hash, never a question's text.
HistoryQuestionSetOut.title: HistoryQuestionSetOut

HistoryScanOut.description: One point on the client's timeline.
HistoryScanOut.title: HistoryScanOut

HistorySentimentOut.description:
How one engine described the subject across one scan's answers — Epic A.

COUNTS, not a rate, and the four buckets are exhaustive over that engine's
answers for the scan. A rate would have to pick a denominator, and the only
honest one here is "answers where the subject was named" — which is exactly
the number `unclassified` reports separately, so a caller can compute any
rate it wants and none is baked in.

`unclassified` is the state the whole product turns on: the subject was not
named, so tone toward it was never asked. It is NOT a neutral. Folding the
two together would report a brand nobody mentioned as having been described
neutrally, which is a measurement nobody took.
HistorySentimentOut.title: HistorySentimentOut

InviteSeatRequest.description:
Invite an address to a seat.

Role defaults to MEMBER, the least-privileged seat there is. An invite form
that defaults to ADMIN is how an agency ends up with five owners.
InviteSeatRequest.title: InviteSeatRequest

InviteSeatResponse.description:
What the invite produced, and what the agency's seat position now is.

`seat_consumed` is false when the address already held an `INVITED` seat and
this call only re-issued its link. The distinction is the difference between
"Invited" and "A new link is on its way", and a screen that cannot tell them
apart will report a seat as newly taken when the count did not move.

`seats` is returned so a caller does not have to re-read `GET /auth/me` to
find out how much room is left after acting.
InviteSeatResponse.title: InviteSeatResponse

MeOut.description:
The whole authenticated context in one call.

The web app needs user, agency, and seat usage to render its shell. Serving
them together avoids three round trips on every page load.
MeOut.title: MeOut

MentionShareOut.description:
One brand's share of the mentions in this scan.

Entity NAMES are facts and are explicitly permitted. `outranks_subject` is
arithmetic over stored ordinals, not a judgement.
MentionShareOut.title: MentionShareOut

OtherSitesOut.description: What the agency has confirmed and dismissed, and what the latest scan suggests.
OtherSitesOut.title: OtherSitesOut

PendingInvitationOut.description:
An invitation that has not been accepted, revoked, or expired.

No token and no URL — see the module docstring.
PendingInvitationOut.title: PendingInvitationOut

PortalSessionOut.description:
Where to send the browser to manage an existing subscription.

Same shape as `CheckoutSessionOut` and deliberately a separate class. They
are two different resources with two different preconditions — a portal
session requires an existing customer and a checkout session creates one —
and collapsing them into a shared `UrlOut` would make the OpenAPI schema
describe them as interchangeable.
PortalSessionOut.title: PortalSessionOut

PromptIntent.description: Buyer-journey stage. §7 Epic 4 requires intent tagging.
PromptIntent.title: PromptIntent

PromptOriginOut.description:
How many of the scan's questions the generator wrote and how many came from templates.

Counts only (F5). Stored on the prompt set when the scan ran (`generation_params`); null on
the report for a scan stored before the counts were recorded.
PromptOriginOut.title: PromptOriginOut

PromptRunBrandOut.description: A brand this answer named, and where it appeared.
PromptRunBrandOut.title: PromptRunBrandOut

PromptRunCitationOut.description: A source this answer cited. Location, never content.
PromptRunCitationOut.title: PromptRunCitationOut

PromptRunHistoryOut.description:
A client's runs, newest first, with what the throttle has left.

`runsRemaining` is served rather than left to the browser to infer. The
ceiling is a server-side decision and a client that guessed it would either
block a legal run or offer one that 429s — both worse than being told.
PromptRunHistoryOut.title: PromptRunHistoryOut

PromptRunIn.description:
The question. Bounded here as well as in the service.

Two checks on purpose: this one rejects an oversized body at the edge before
it is read, and `normalise_prompt` rejects one that only becomes oversized
after whitespace is collapsed. Neither subsumes the other.
PromptRunIn.title: PromptRunIn

PromptRunResultOut.description: What one engine did with the prompt.
PromptRunResultOut.title: PromptRunResultOut

PromptRunStatus.description:
A run's overall verdict, from its per-engine outcomes.

The same three-way shape `terminal_status_for` gives a scan, and for the
same reason: PARTIAL exists so the screen can say "one engine was down"
rather than presenting a narrower result as if it were the whole picture.
PromptRunStatus.title: PromptRunStatus

PromptShelfOut.description:
One answer, as the ordered shelf of brands it named — Epic 7.1.

Direction A of `design-direction.md` §5. The report's aggregate tables
answer "how often overall"; this answers "in THIS question, who stood
where, and were you there at all". The subject's absence is a fact this
row carries explicitly (`subject_present: false`) rather than an entry
that is merely missing, because the visualisation draws absence as an
empty notch and a silently absent row would draw nothing.

On `prompt_text` — the facts-only rule governs scraped and model-returned
content ABOUT third parties. This is OUR OWN generated question, the same
field `PromptOut.text` has returned on `/scans/{id}/prompts` since Epic 4,
and the exception is registered by name in `test_facts_only.py` rather than
left to dodge the forbidden-field sweep by luck.
PromptShelfOut.title: PromptShelfOut

ProposedSiteOut.description:
A domain the latest finished scan cited that carries a brand's name under another suffix.

A proposal, not a finding: it counts as the brand's own only once it is confirmed, and
asking about it changes nothing.
ProposedSiteOut.title: ProposedSiteOut

QuestionSetOut.description:
Which questions the scan asked: the client's earlier set again, or a new one (F6).

`reused` is true for a set copied from an earlier scan, and `source_scan_date` is the day (UTC)
that scan finished, else started, else was asked for: a day, never a time of day. It is null
for a new set, and when the source scan is gone or is not this client's own. Null on the
report for a scan stored before the set was fingerprinted. Not sensitive: the questions are
ours and the day is a scan's, so the shared report carries it as well.
QuestionSetOut.title: QuestionSetOut

ReplaceCompetitorsRequest.description:
Operator override for a detected competitor set.

Replaces the set wholesale rather than patching individual rows: an operator
correcting a bad detection is expressing "these are the rivals", and
reconciling that against auto-detected rows one at a time invites a
half-applied state where the correction is neither in force nor discarded.

Every competitor supplied here is marked `isManualOverride`, which protects
it from being removed by a later re-detection.
ReplaceCompetitorsRequest.title: ReplaceCompetitorsRequest

ReplaceOtherSitesRequest.description:
All three lists, replaced: the client's confirmed sites, the rivals', and the dismissed.

Every list is named, so a request that leaves one out is refused rather than read as
"clear it". A rival left out of `rivals` has its sites cleared, as a site left out of a list
is removed. How many sites a brand may have, and which domains may be on which list, is
checked in `services/other_sites.py`, which says why in a sentence naming the domain.
ReplaceOtherSitesRequest.title: ReplaceOtherSitesRequest

ReportAgencyOut.description:
The white-label surface — Epic 9.22.

The written policy this docstring used to be waiting for now exists, and it
is short: an agency may change a logo and ONE colour, and that colour is
confined to chrome. `--avp-vis-*`, `--avp-beacon-*`,
`--avp-competitor-{1..5}` and the semantic four are not overridable by any
code path, because the report's palette is notation rather than decoration
and an agency free to recolour it changes what the score means.

**There is no field here that can reach an encoded token**, which is the
guarantee — a type, not a convention. `accentColor` is chrome only, and
`AgencyBranding.test.tsx` asserts it never renders adjacent to one.

No `customDomain`: deferred, and `schemas/agency.py` says why.
ReportAgencyOut.title: ReportAgencyOut

ReportAuditFindingOut.description:
An audit check the report can act on.

Same shape as `AuditCheckOut` — a machine `detail_code`, never prose. The
fix beat maps the code to concrete copy from our own string table.
ReportAuditFindingOut.title: ReportAuditFindingOut

ReportCompetitorOut.description:
A detected competitor plus its comparable sub-scores.

**No composite, deliberately.** Sentiment is classified toward the subject
only and Technical Foundation is the subject's own site, so 25% of the
weight has no per-competitor input. A "competitor composite" over the
remaining 75% would not be comparable to the subject's — it would read as a
competitor scoring lower than they do. The report compares per-dimension
instead, on the three dimensions that genuinely have both sides.

Null sub-scores mean the scan produced no comparison for this competitor.

`average_position` / `position_count` are reported, not scored — see
`CompetitorScoreOut`. Null when never named on an awareness prompt.
ReportCompetitorOut.title: ReportCompetitorOut

ReportDimensionOut.description:
One §6 dimension as the report needs it.

`key` is a stable machine key; the human label lives in the frontend string
table, matching how `detail_code` is handled (api-contracts.md, Epic 6).

An EXCLUDED dimension carries `included: false`, a null `subscore`, and the
reason. It is never emitted as `subscore: 0` — the whole point of
`excluded_dimensions` is that "nothing to measure" and "measured, scored
zero" are different claims about a client.
ReportDimensionOut.title: ReportDimensionOut

ReportOut.description: Everything the five narrative beats need, in one response.
ReportOut.title: ReportOut

ReportProofOut.description:
The evidence beat's raw material — all of it aggregated counts.

This is the surface the facts-only rule is most exposed on, because it is the
first time collected facts are RENDERED rather than stored. There is no
field here that could hold an engine's prose, and there is nothing upstream
to fill one with: `engine_results` has no text-bearing column at all.
ReportProofOut.title: ReportProofOut

ReportSubjectOut.description: Who the report is about. Facts from Client (Epic 2).
ReportSubjectOut.title: ReportSubjectOut

ResetPasswordConfirm.description:
Redeem a link and set a new password.

The password rules are the SIGN-UP rules, reused rather than restated —
same length bounds and the same repetitiveness check. A reset path with
weaker rules than registration is a way in, not a convenience.
ResetPasswordConfirm.title: ResetPasswordConfirm

ResetPasswordRequest.description: Ask for a reset link. The response is identical whoever this is.
ResetPasswordRequest.title: ResetPasswordRequest

ResetRequestOut.description:
The answer to a reset request — the same for every address.

`email_configured` is a fact about the DEPLOYMENT, never about the address:
whether this service can send email at all. It exists so the screen can
stop saying "check your inbox" when nothing was sent (2026-09-29), and it
cannot become an enumeration oracle, because no address changes it.
ResetRequestOut.title: ResetRequestOut

RivalSitesIn.description: The other sites confirmed for one rival, named by the rival's own domain.
RivalSitesIn.title: RivalSitesIn

RivalSuggestionOut.description:
A domain the latest scan's answers named, offered to the agency as a rival.

A suggestion, not a finding: it changes nothing until the agency adds it through
`PUT /clients/{clientId}/competitors`, and asking about it writes nothing.
RivalSuggestionOut.title: RivalSuggestionOut

RivalSuggestionsOut.description: The suggestions for one client, most cited first, then by domain. Empty if there are none.
RivalSuggestionsOut.title: RivalSuggestionsOut

RunScanRequest.description:
Start a scan.

`promptLimit` caps the generated set. It exists for cost control during
verification — a full run is 20-30 prompts across every engine, and the
grounded engine can take 100s per prompt. Omit it for a real scan.

`engines` is de-duplicated BEFORE validation and bounded by the enum's own
size — API key discipline audit, 2026-09-07. Neither alone bounds spend: a
bare `max_length` still lets `["claude", "claude", "claude"]` through as
three billed calls per prompt that then die on
`uq_engine_results_prompt_engine` after the money is spent, and
de-duplication is a ceiling only because the enum is finite. Together they
make "one call per engine per prompt" true by construction. Whether each
engine has an ADAPTER is the router's check, against `ENGINE_REGISTRY`:
the enum names what this product might ever measure, the registry what it
can measure today.
RunScanRequest.title: RunScanRequest

ScanEmailsOut.description:
The scan-finished email switch, for the signed-in caller only (F1, 2026-10-06).

`available` is a fact about the deployment: `EMAIL_SCAN_NOTIFICATIONS` is on AND email is
configured, the same for every user. `enabled` is this caller's own choice.
ScanEmailsOut.title: ScanEmailsOut

ScanEmailsRequest.description: Set your own choice. Strict (a JSON true or false) and nothing else may be in the body.
ScanEmailsRequest.title: ScanEmailsRequest

SeatListOut.description:
Everyone occupying a seat, plus the invitations still outstanding.

Both lists, not one merged list. A pending invitee appears in `members`
with `status: "invited"` because they occupy a seat and that is what the
seat count is about; they appear again in `invitations` because only that
row knows when the link expires. Merging them would force one of those two
facts to be dropped.
SeatListOut.title: SeatListOut

SetAutoRescanRequest.description: Switch "Rescan every month" on or off for one client.
SetAutoRescanRequest.title: SetAutoRescanRequest

ShareLinkOut.description:
The public link for a report — Epic 9.8.

Carries the complete URL, not just the token, because the operator's next
action is to paste it into an email. Returning a bare token would force
every caller to rebuild the same string, which is how a frontend and a
backend end up disagreeing about a path.

`token` is exposed alongside it deliberately: it is the operator's OWN
capability for their OWN scan, already implied by the URL beside it, and
tests assert on it without having to parse a URL apart.

`expiresAt` is returned because the operator is about to paste this URL
into an email and the one thing they cannot see from the URL is when it
stops working — Epic 9.21. It is the end the link was given when it was
made: a press on a live link returns the same value, and only a press when
no link is live (never shared, withdrawn, or ended) makes a new link with a
fresh 30 days (checklist 3.28).
ShareLinkOut.title: ShareLinkOut

SharedReportRequest.description:
The body of `POST /reports/shared` and `POST /reports/shared/pdf`.

The share token travels here, not in the URL path, so it never reaches a
request log. The bounds are the same ones every other token body uses

get.description:
This agency's subscription, as recorded, and its scan allowance. **Never asks Stripe.**

The allowance — `scansUsedThisPeriod`, `scanLimit`, `periodResetsAt` — is
one COUNT over the agency's scans (2026-09-28, `services/scan_allowance`).
`scanLimit` is null when billing is not configured on this deployment,
which is the honest way to say no gate applies. `freeScanRequiresGoogle`
(2026-09-29) is true when the free scan is what this sign-in would start
and it has no linked Google identity — the case a scan start refuses with
`SCAN_LIMIT_VERIFY_REQUIRED`. It is about the requesting user, not the
agency: two seats of one agency can read it differently.

`cancelAtPeriodEnd` (2026-09-29) is true when the subscription was
cancelled in Stripe's portal and runs to `currentPeriodEnd` without
renewing. It is still `active` until then, so `isActive` stays true and
the scan allowance stays the plan's.

`trialEndsAt` (2026-10-04) is when the free trial ends and the card is first
charged, and is set ONLY while the status is `trialing`: null for every other
status, for a trial that converted (the date is history) and for an agency that
never had one. A trialing agency is `isActive` and has the plan's full allowance.

`trialEligible` (2026-10-04, round two) is whether Settings may promise this agency a free
trial: true only when a trial is on (`STRIPE_TRIAL_DAYS` above 0 and billing configured) and
the agency's own row has never had a subscription, the same row test checkout applies. **It
cannot see Stripe's side of that test** (the customer's subscription list: a read never
asks Stripe), so true means "nothing in our record says no": checkout can still refuse the
trial to a customer Stripe remembers an ended subscription for.

**Both trial fields are about the REQUESTING user** (2026-10-05, founder decision 3.72): a
trial needs a verified Google identity on the user who starts checkout, so two seats of
one agency can read them differently. `trialEligible` is true only when the agency's
record allows a trial (above) AND this user has a linked Google identity: it is what a
Subscribe from this sign-in would get. `trialRequiresGoogle` is true exactly when the
record allows a trial and the ONLY thing missing is that identity: checkout would give
this user no trial, and continuing with Google on the same address would. The two are
never both true.

Every field comes off the `agencies` row the webhook maintains. A settings
screen that called a payment processor on page load would be slower, would
fail whenever Stripe was slow, and would put a third party in the render
path of a page with four other sections on it — for a value that would be
no more current than the webhook already makes it.

The agency is already loaded on the principal, so there is no query here at
all beyond the one `current_principal` performs on every request.

**Errors:** `401`, `403` (member role), `404` (another agency's id).

post.description:
Create a Stripe Checkout Session. Returns the URL to navigate to.

**`201`, because a session really is created** — at Stripe, with an id and a
lifetime, and this call is what makes it. That it lives in someone else's
database does not make it less of a created resource.

The agency's Stripe customer is created here too, if it does not have one
yet, and REUSED if it does. A second visit to this endpoint does not mint a
second customer — see `services/billing.py`, where the reuse and the unique
constraint under it are explained.

**This endpoint does not subscribe anybody.** It returns a URL. The
subscription begins when Stripe says it did, over the webhook below.

**A free trial, when `STRIPE_TRIAL_DAYS` is above 0** (2026-10-04): the session
asks Stripe for that many trial days and for the card at checkout, and Stripe
charges when the trial ends unless the agency cancels. One trial per agency, ever:
an agency that has had any subscription, or whose Stripe customer has, gets the
plain checkout. **And only for a user with a linked Google identity** (2026-10-05):
the rule is on the user who starts the checkout, not the agency, so a password-only
user gets the plain checkout (no trial, the same session otherwise). The response is
the same either way, a URL.

**Errors:**

- `401`, `403` (member role), `404` (another agency's id). Authority and
  tenancy are settled first, so a member or another agency never sees a `409`.
- `409 subscription-already-active` when the agency's status is `active` or
  `trialing`.
- `409 subscription-needs-attention` when it is anything else that is not
  over: `past_due`, `unpaid`, `paused`, `incomplete`, or a status this server
  has never seen (it denies by default). Those are live at Stripe, so a
  second checkout would create a second subscription; the detail points at
  Manage billing in Settings and carries no Stripe id and not the status.
  Only no subscription, `canceled` and `incomplete_expired` may check out.
- The stored status is checked first, before any Stripe call. When the
  agency already has a customer, Stripe is then asked: its open Checkout
  Sessions are expired FIRST and its subscriptions listed AFTER, so both
  subscription refusals also fire when our row has not caught up (or says
  `canceled`), and a session paid in the meantime is found.
- `409 checkout-in-progress` when another checkout holds the agency row for
  over 3 s. Nothing was created; retrying is safe.
- `503 service-unavailable`, with a sentence that says which step: Stripe
  failed while listing or expiring the open sessions, or there are more of
  them than one page holds; or Stripe failed while listing the
  subscriptions, or a full page of them had none live on it (a live one
  could be on the next page). A full page with a live subscription on it is
  still the `409`. Nothing is created in any of these.
- `503 billing-not-configured` when `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` or `STRIPE_PRICE_ID`
  is unset, carrying a detail that names the variable.
- `503 plan-price-mismatch` when the latest price check found the Price is not
  the plan (amount, currency, interval or archived) and a fresh read made for
  this request confirms it. Checked after the two `409` refusals and before
  anything is created at Stripe. A price read that fails never refuses.

409.description: Checkout cannot start. One of three problem types: `/problems/subscription-already-active` (the agency already has an active or trialing subscription), `/problems/subscription-needs-attention` (it has one that is still live at Stripe but not paid up: past_due, unpaid, paused, incomplete, or any status that is not over), or `/problems/checkout-in-progress` (another checkout for this agency holds its row lock; retry in a moment).

post.description:
Create a Stripe Billing Portal session. Returns the URL to navigate to.

Update a card, cancel, download invoices — Stripe's own hosted screens, for
one API call and no UI here. Building those would mean handling card
details, dunning and invoice PDFs, which is a product rather than a feature,
and one that already exists.

Nothing is written, so nothing is committed. The `201` is for the session
created at Stripe, exactly as above.

**Errors:** `401`, `403`, `404`, `503 billing-not-configured` — including
when the agency has never subscribed and so has no customer for the portal
to be about.

patch.description:
Set this agency's logo and accent colour — Epic 9.22.

**What may be changed is a logo and ONE colour, and the colour only reaches
chrome.** The report's palette is notation rather than decoration: the
visibility ramp encodes the score, the competitor series is neutral by
design, the beacon marks the subject being scanned, and the semantic four
say a scan failed. `BrandingRequest` has no field that can reach any of
them — the guarantee is the type, not this docstring.

**Admin or owner, not any member.** How every report an agency sends is
branded is an agency-level decision with an external audience, which is the
same bar `PATCH`-ing seats sits behind.

**PATCH, and null means remove.** An agency that set the wrong logo needs a
way back to unbranded; a route that can only ever set is a one-way door.
Both fields are independent, so sending one does not clear the other —
which is why the body is read field by field rather than assigned wholesale.

**`404` for another agency's id**, never `403`: answering "you may not
touch that agency" confirms it exists.

**Errors:** `401`, `403` (member seat), `404` (another agency's id), `422`
(a logo URL that is not `https://`, or a colour that is not `#rrggbb`).

post.description:
Invite an address to a seat.

**The seat limit is enforced here, server-side, in the same transaction as
the insert.** `GET /auth/me`'s `seats` object lets a screen grey out the
form when the agency is full, but that is a courtesy — the limit is
commercial policy and a client-side check is a suggestion. Refused with
`409 /problems/seat-limit-reached`, carrying `seatsUsed` and `seatLimit` so
the screen can say what to do about it rather than just that it failed.

**Re-inviting an address that already holds an INVITED seat is allowed** and
consumes no second seat: it revokes the outstanding link and mints a new
one. `seatConsumed: false` in the response says that is what happened. See
`services/invitations.py` for why refusing it would be a trap.

**`201` in both cases.** An invitation row is genuinely created either way —
that is the resource this endpoint makes. Whether a SEAT was newly consumed
is a different question and it is answered in the body, not in the status.

**`acceptUrl`, only when email is not configured** (2026-09-29). Without
email the invitee would never hear about the seat, so the link comes back
here, once, to the owner or admin who made it, to send themselves. With
email configured it is null and the link goes to the invitee's inbox only.

**Errors:** `401`, `403`, `404` (another agency's id), `409
seat-limit-reached`, `409 email-already-registered` (a live account, here or
elsewhere), `422`.

get.description:
Who holds a seat, and which invitations are still live.

`GET /auth/me` already carries `seats: {used, limit}` — the COUNT. It has
never carried the roster, because the shell needs a number and not a list,
and a management screen needs the list. This is that list.

**Errors:** `401`, `403` (member role), `404` (another agency's id).

post.description:
Mark an alert as seen.

**Idempotent**: acknowledging an already-acknowledged alert returns the
original timestamp rather than moving it. An operator double-clicking must
not rewrite when they first saw something.

There is deliberately no un-acknowledge. Dismissing is a record that a
person looked, and a log an operator can quietly un-read is not a log.

Scoped by `agency_id` on the row itself — the denormalised column exists so
this is one predicate rather than a join through the client.

Change your own password while signed in. **Auth required.**

The current password is re-verified server-side. A session proves somebody
got in once; it does not prove they are still the account holder, and an
unlocked laptop or a stolen cookie presents a perfectly valid one.

EVERY OTHER SESSION IS REVOKED. THIS ONE IS NOT.
------------------------------------------------
**This is not the reset flow's answer copied over.** `reset-password/confirm`
revokes everything and leaves the caller signed OUT, because the person
holding a reset link proved control of an inbox rather than knowledge of a
password — they may be recovering from a compromise, they might not be the
account holder at all, and making them sign in once with the new password
confirms they hold it.

Neither of those applies here. The caller just demonstrated knowledge of the
current password, so the caller is not the suspect and signing them out of
the session they are actively using would be friction with no security
value — the same argument api-contracts.md already makes for signing a user
in at sign-up.

The OTHER sessions are a different question, and the answer is still revoke.
The commonest reason someone changes a password while signed in is that they
think somebody else has it; a change that left every other device alive
would fail at the one job the user believed they were doing. `logout-all`
exists for the explicit version, but requiring two deliberate actions to
accomplish the obvious intent of one is a trap.

So: `revoke_all_for_user`, then a FRESH session for this caller and a new
cookie. Every other device is signed out; this one keeps working. The new
token is minted rather than the old one spared, because "spare this digest"
is a special case in the revocation path and a bulk revoke with an exception
in it is the kind of code that later fails to revoke.

**Errors:** `401 authentication-required` (no session), `401
invalid-credentials` (wrong current password — no "no such user" branch
exists, because the caller is authenticated), `422 validation-failed` for a
new password that fails the SIGN-UP rules or that is the current one, `429
rate-limited` (10 failed attempts per account and 30 per IP per 15 minutes,
counted before the password is verified; a success gives its attempt back),
`503` (Redis down).

get.description:
Where Google sends the browser back. **No auth.** Always a 302.

In order: the state must be one this process minted and not yet used;
the flow cookie must be the one `/start` set in this browser (else
`browser-mismatch`); the code is exchanged and the ID token verified (signature, audience,
issuer, expiry); the token's nonce must be the state's; then the
linking policy decides. Three destinations:

- an existing account → the session cookie is set and the browser goes
  to `/dashboard`;
- a new address → a ten-minute ticket is minted and the browser goes to
  `/sign-up/google#ticket=…` (the fragment, never the query, so it is in
  no request log and no Referer) to name the agency;
- anything else → `/?google=error&reason=…` with one of `not-configured`,
  `denied`, `invalid-state`, `browser-mismatch`, `exchange-failed`, `email-unverified`,
  `account-suspended`, `email-claimed`, `invitation-expired`,
  `account-unavailable`, or `unavailable` when something this route
  depends on — Redis, Postgres, the session store — failed underneath it
  (2026-09-21; until then that was the one way this route showed a raw
  500 page).

**Errors:** none as status codes. A person arriving here is not a script
and gets a page, not a problem document.

post.description:
Create the agency and its owner from a verified Google identity. **No auth.**

The Google half of `/sign-up`: same agency, same owner seat, same
sign-in-on-creation, no password. The ticket is consumed here, so the
page it came from cannot create two agencies.

**Errors:** `400 invalid-google-ticket`, `409 email-already-registered`
(the address was registered in the minutes since the ticket was minted),
`422`.

What the completion page shows before asking for an agency name. **No auth.**

A POST so the ticket rides in the body: it is a bearer credential with a
session token's entropy, and a URL is logged. It is not a mutation: the
ticket is read without being consumed, so asking twice is not a second
sign-in. The web page removes the ticket from the address bar once read
(like invite and reset), so reloading that page does not bring it back and
the person starts again. `GET` with a `?ticket=` is `405`.

The ticket is bound to the browser that signed in: the flow cookie must
come with it.

**Errors:** `400 invalid-google-ticket` for unknown, used, expired and
another browser's alike.

get.description:
Send the browser to Google. **No auth.** A navigation, not an API call.

Mints a `state`, a `nonce` and a PKCE verifier, parks them in Redis for
ten minutes, and redirects to Google's authorization endpoint with the
state, the nonce and the S256 challenge. The state is looked up
server-side; the flow cookie set here, whose digest is parked with it,
ties it to this browser and is compared at the callback.

**Errors:** `503 google-sign-in-not-configured` when the deployment has
no OAuth client. The web app shows the button regardless; this is what
it gets until the founder creates one.

post.description:
Redeem a seat invitation, set a password, and sign in. **No auth.**

Unauthenticated by necessity: the person holding this link has no account
to authenticate with yet. That is what the link is for.

**This signs them in — unlike the reset path, and for the reason sign-up
gives.** `reset-password/confirm` deliberately leaves the caller signed out
because they proved control of an inbox rather than knowledge of a
password, and one deliberate sign-in confirms they hold the new one. There
is no prior state to protect here: this is a first password on a seat that
has never been used, exactly the situation api-contracts.md already calls
"friction with no security value" on the sign-up path.

**`200`, not `201`.** Nothing is created. The `User` row was inserted when
the invitation was sent and has occupied a seat ever since; this fills it.

**Errors:** `400 invalid-invitation` for unknown, expired, already-accepted,
revoked, and pointing-at-a-seat-that-has-since-been-removed alike — one
response, no branch that says which. `422` for a password that fails the
same rules sign-up applies.
Revoke every session for the caller, on every device.

get.description:
The signed-in context, in one call. **Auth required.**

`feedbackEmail` (2026-10-06) is `FEEDBACK_EMAIL`, null when it is unset: the address the
shell's "Send feedback" link writes to. It is on this response, and on the other responses
that return the same context to someone who has just signed in, and on no other.

put.description:
Turn the emails sent when a scan you started finishes on or off. **Auth required.**

**Only your own choice.** There is no user id anywhere in the request: the row written is the
caller's, matched by user id AND agency id, and a body that names anything but `enabled` is a
`422`. Accepted whether or not the feature is on (`available` in the answer says), because it
writes one boolean nothing reads while the feature is off. Idempotent.

**Errors:** `401 authentication-required`, `422 validation-failed` (not a JSON true or false).

post.description:
Redeem a reset link and set the new password.

**Every existing session is revoked.** A reset is what someone does when
they believe the account is compromised, so leaving the attacker's session
alive would defeat the exercise. `logout-all` already exists for the
deliberate version of this; here it is not optional.

The caller is NOT signed in afterwards, deliberately — unlike sign-up. The
person holding this link proved control of an inbox, not knowledge of the
old password, and making them sign in once with the new one confirms they
have it.

**Errors:** `400 invalid-reset-token` for unknown, expired, already-used,
and belonging-to-an-inactive-user alike — one response, no branch that says
which.

post.description:
Ask for a reset link. **Always `200`, and the same body for every address.**

The response is byte-identical whether the address has an account, has a
suspended one, or has never been seen. Any observable difference is an
oracle for enumerating who banks here, which is precisely what
`authenticate` already burns a dummy Argon2 hash to avoid on the login path.

**It does differ by deployment, honestly** (2026-09-29): `emailConfigured`
says whether this service can send email at all, and the `detail` says
what that means. With no `RESEND_API_KEY` nothing is sent — and nothing is
logged in its place any more, because the link it used to log is a live
credential. Neither field depends on the address.

The email is best-effort by construction: `send_password_reset` never raises
and never reports its outcome, so a provider outage cannot become a
different status code.

**Errors:** `429` when the per-email or per-IP limit is spent. The per-email
limit trips identically for every address, so it reveals nothing about
accounts. `422` if the body is not an email address.

Create an agency and its owner, then sign them straight in.

Signing in as part of signup is deliberate: requiring a fresh login
immediately after choosing a password is friction with no security value.

get.description:
What the plan offers the public: the length of its free trial. **No auth, no agency, no
secrets.**

`trialDays` is `STRIPE_TRIAL_DAYS` (2026-10-04), 0 meaning there is no trial. The public
pricing card and landing page read it and say "the first N days after you subscribe are
free" only for an N above 0, so the number is stated in one place and a page never claims
a trial that checkout would not give. It is 0 wherever checkout cannot start a subscription (the
Stripe key or the Price unset), and while the page is still asking, or the answer fails,
the page says nothing about a trial at all.

It touches no database and no Stripe, so it is as cheap as `/health`, and there is nothing
in it to limit or to guess. It describes the offer to a NEW agency: whether a particular
agency still gets the trial is its own history, decided by checkout.

**Never cached** (`Cache-Control: no-store`): a short cache would keep a page saying
"30 days free" for its length after a deploy turned the trial off. A GET is not checked by
the Origin check, and CORS is unchanged: the web app reads it same-origin through its
`/api/v1` proxy, and a page on any other origin is not let read the answer.

**Errors:** none of its own.

post.description:
Stripe telling us what happened. **The only writer of subscription state.**

**No session auth, and that is not a hole.** The caller is a machine with no
account; what authenticates it is an HMAC over the exact bytes of this
request body, keyed on `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. That is a stronger claim
than a session cookie makes, because it is a claim about the payload and not
merely about the sender.

**The raw body is read, not a parsed model.** `await request.body()` rather
than a Pydantic parameter, because the signature covers the bytes Stripe
sent. Letting FastAPI parse and re-serialise first would verify a signature
against a payload that is equal as JSON and different as bytes, which fails
for something as ordinary as key order. This is the single most common way
webhook verification is written wrongly, and it fails closed and confusingly
rather than obviously.

**With no secret configured this refuses.** `503`, naming the variable, and
it does not fall back to trusting the body — see `verify_webhook`, which
explains why this is the opposite of the answer `services/email.py` gives
for its own unset key.

**An unrecognised event type is a `200`.** Stripe sends whatever the account
is configured to send, and answering non-2xx to an event nobody wants makes
Stripe retry it, back off, and eventually mark the endpoint unhealthy —
which degrades delivery of the events that DO matter. The body says whether
it was acted on, so a human reading `stripe listen` output can tell the
difference between "handled" and "politely ignored".

**Idempotent and ordered.** Each handled event id is recorded once; a
redelivery answers `{"received": true, "handled": false, "duplicate": true}`
and applies nothing. An event older than the agency's newest applied one
answers `{"received": true, "handled": false, "stale": true}` and applies
nothing. Unmatched and unhandled events answer `handled: false` alone.

**`customer.subscription.trial_will_end`** (2026-10-04) answers `handled: true`
and does nothing but log (`billing.trial_will_end`, ids only): no state, no
watermark, no ledger row.

**Errors:** `400 invalid-webhook-signature` for a missing, malformed or
wrong signature, and for a body that is not JSON. `503
billing-not-configured` when `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset.

get.description:
Cursor-paginated client list, newest first.

IDs are ULIDs, so `id < cursor ORDER BY id DESC` is a stable, index-backed
window that does not skip or repeat rows when something is inserted
mid-scroll — which for an active prospecting list is the common case.

post.description:
Submit a URL: creates the client, crawls it, and classifies its industry.

Runs synchronously. §7's acceptance criterion is a classified industry
within 30 seconds of submitting a URL, and the measured path is a few
seconds, so one round trip is both sufficient and simpler than polling.

Set `classify: false` to create the record without spending an LLM call.

**One site read per agency at a time, and four at once** (2026-10-02). With
classification on, this request reads the site in the API's one browser. An agency
may have one such read queued or running at once, counted here, on
`POST /clients/{clientId}/reclassify` and on `POST /scans/{scanId}/audit` together,
and only four agencies at once. Past either limit the request is refused before
anything is created. A read that waits more than a minute for the browser is
refused the same way, and writes nothing: no client is created.

**Errors:** `429 rate-limited` (with `Retry-After: 60`): "Your agency already has a
site being read. Try again in a minute." or "The crawler is busy with other pages
right now. Try again in a minute."; `409 invalid-url`; `409 conflict`;
`422 validation-failed`.

get.description:
What this client's robots.txt asks each AI crawler to do — Epic F.

**Reads. Fetches nothing.** The verdicts were parsed during the scan's
technical audit, from the robots.txt it already fetched, and persisted
then. Re-fetching here would make the same URL answer differently between
two page loads and would mean this endpoint could be used to make the API
issue outbound requests on demand.

**This answers "can an AI crawler read this site", not "is one reading
it".** Server logs would answer the second and nothing in this system
ingests them; `services/ai_crawlers.py` records the correction in full.
No field in the response can be rendered as activity.

`scanId` selects one scan; without it the newest scan carrying a policy is
used. The response carries `availableScanIds` so a picker needs no second
call — the same contract `answer-gaps` uses.

Returns `null` — not 404 — when no scan of this client has ever recorded a
policy, which is every scan predating this feature. A client with nothing
to show is a normal state on a screen that has an empty view for it, not a
missing resource.

Scoped to the caller's agency by `get_client`, which 404s rather than 403s
on another agency's id.

get.description:
This client's alerts, newest first.

**Newest first**, unlike `GET /clients/{id}/history`. That one is a trend
and a trend reads left to right from its earliest point; this is a LOG an
operator checks, and the thing they are looking for is the most recent
entry. `prompt-runs` orders itself the same way for the same reason.

**Reads only.** Alerts are generated once at the end of a scan (see
`services/alerts.py`), never recomputed here — an alert that re-derived on
every request could appear and disappear between two page loads of the same
data, and an acknowledgement would have nothing stable to attach to.

`scansTotal` and `scansCompared` are returned because an empty feed is
ambiguous on its own: most clients have one scan and can never have an
alert. Reporting only "0 alerts" would read as an all-clear the data cannot
support.

**A visibility alert from a FAILED scan is left out** (3.30, extending
3.24). It quotes that scan's composite, and a failed scan has no score that
is ever shown. Alerts are written before the scan's final status is stamped,
so a scan that then ends failed can already have one. This route does not
delete or change the row; the feed does not list it, `unacknowledged` and
`scansCompared` do not count it, and nothing quotes it. The other kinds are
not about the score and are listed as before.

Scoped to the caller's agency by `get_client`, which 404s rather than 403s
on another agency's id.

Prompts where a rival was named and this client was not — Epic B.

**Reads. Collects nothing, calls no engine and no model, writes nothing.**
Every figure is an aggregation over `engine_result_brand_mentions` and
`engine_result_citations` rows some earlier scan already persisted.

`scanId` selects one scan; without it the newest griddable scan is used.

post.description:
Run SERP + AI co-citation discovery and rank the top competitors.

Runs synchronously. A run makes several paid SerpApi searches and several
model calls, so it is explicitly operator-triggered rather than implicit in
intake — an accidental re-detection costs money.

**For paying agencies since 2026-10-04** (launch checklist 3.61, the founder's
decision). The 24-hour limit below caps a client, not an agency, and every run is
paid searches, so the route is for an agency whose subscription is `active` or
`trialing`, and for the platform operator (a listed address with a linked Google
identity, the scan allowance's own exemption). Anyone else is refused with
`402 subscription-required` and one plain sentence that names no status and no code.
Where billing is not configured the route stays open, as the scan allowance does. It
is checked after the client is found, so another agency's client is still a `404`
whatever the caller's plan, and before the day below is taken, so a refused press
spends none of the client's day: no search is made and no scan is opened. A scan's own
detection is not this route and is unaffected: a client with no competitor set gets
one when it is first scanned, on any plan.

**Once per client per 24 hours** (2026-10-03, launch checklist 3.53), for those who
are allowed. The day is taken when a run starts, so a run that then fails still
counts: its searches may already be spent. Checked after the client is found, so
another agency's client is still a `404` and cannot spend this client's day, and
before anything is done. Another client of the same agency has its own day. A scan's
own detection, for a client with no competitor set yet, is never refused by this
limit and does not use the day up; neither does replacing the set by hand with `PUT`.

Competitors an operator marked as overrides are preserved across runs.

**Where the result goes (launch checklist 3.78/3.79).** Into the client's NEXT LIST: the list
the next scan that starts will adopt, which is what this answers (`scanId` is null, because it
belongs to no scan yet). A scan's own set never changes once the scan has started, so a run
does not touch a finished scan's set and does not touch a running scan's either. With no next
list yet, one is made as a copy of the client's latest set and detection merges into the
copy, so rivals an operator named or struck stay named and struck; a client with no set at all
starts from an empty list. The open scan this route opens (or reuses, as before) carries no
set until it runs.

**Errors:** `401 authentication-required`; `402 subscription-required` ("Running
competitor detection on its own needs an active subscription. A scan still finds a
client's competitors the first time it runs."); `404 not-found`; `429 rate-limited`
(with `Retry-After`, the whole seconds left in the 24 hours): "Competitor detection
already ran for this client in the last 24 hours. It can run again in about N hours."
(the last hour reads "in under an hour"); `503 service-unavailable` (Redis cannot say
whether the day is taken, so nothing runs).

get.description:
Every scan of this client that produced a reading, oldest first.

**Reads. Collects nothing, writes nothing, computes no new figure.** It
exists because the two trends a client's space shows are not both available
as stored columns: cited-domain counts aggregate persisted citation rows,
while the per-rival comparison is derived on read by design and has no
column at all (see `services/client_history.py` for the measurements that
ruled out calling the report endpoint N times instead).

Scoped to the caller's agency by `get_client`, which 404s rather than 403s
on another agency's id — the same rule every other client route follows, so
the endpoint cannot be used to probe whether an id exists elsewhere.

What is confirmed, dismissed and proposed as this brand's other sites.

**Reads. Writes nothing.** A proposal changes nothing: a domain counts as a brand's own only
once it is on a confirmed list.

`confirmed` is the client's own confirmed sites, then those of each active rival of the list
the client's NEXT scan will use (its next list if it has one, else the latest scan's set), in
rank order. `proposals` come from the client's latest FINISHED scan (succeeded or partial,
with answered results): each domain its answered results cited that carries the client's name,
or the first rival's in rank order, under another public suffix, counted per domain, most
cited first. The client's and the rivals' own domains and anything already confirmed or
dismissed are not proposed, whichever way each is spelled (`bücher.de` and `xn--bcher-kva.de`
are one host). `dismissed` is one list per client, for the client and its rivals alike. A
client with no finished scan has no proposals, and one with no rivals list has only its own.

`confirmed` and `dismissed` are returned as they are stored, in the DNS form (lower case
ASCII: `xn--bcher-kva.at` for `bücher.at`). A proposal keeps the spelling the engine
cited, which is the domain it cited.

**Errors:** `401`; `404` (another agency's client is the same `404` as an unknown one).

put.description:
Replace the confirmed sites of the client and its rivals, and the dismissed domains.

All three lists are replaced and all three are named: a rival left out of `rivals` has its
sites cleared. The answer is the body of `GET`.

Every domain is stored in the DNS form (lower case ASCII, an internationalised label
IDNA-encoded: `bücher.at` is stored as `xn--bcher-kva.at`) and compared in it, so
`bücher.de` and `xn--bcher-kva.de` are one host: it is listed once, it is a brand's own
domain, and it cannot be both confirmed and dismissed, whichever way each is spelled, and
saving a host again in the other spelling changes nothing. A rival is named by its
`rivalDomain` in either spelling. The answer is what is stored.

The client's confirmed sites and the dismissed list are the client's own. A rival's sites are
written to its row on the client's NEXT LIST, never to a scan's own set: the list the next

the set it started with. A save that changes no rival's sites makes no list.

While the client's most recent scan is RUNNING the answer is `409` and nothing is written, as

**Errors:** `401`; `404`; `409` ("A scan of this client is running."); `422`, with one plain

(`confirmed_and_dismissed`). Nothing is written when any is refused.

Re-run crawl and classification for an existing client.

Needed because a site changes, and because an AMBIGUOUS result is often
worth retrying after the operator has looked at the site themselves.

**One site read per agency at a time, and four at once** (2026-10-02), shared with
`POST /clients` and `POST /scans/{scanId}/audit`: while the agency's other read is
queued or running, or four agencies' reads are, this is a `429`. Checked after the
client is found, so another agency's client is still a `404`. A read that waits
more than a minute for the browser is refused with a `429` too, and the client
keeps the classification it had.

**Errors:** `404 not-found`; `429 rate-limited` (with `Retry-After: 60`).

Domains the latest scan's answers named that the agency may want as rivals.

**Reads. Writes nothing.** A suggestion changes nothing: a domain is a rival only once the
agency adds it through `PUT /clients/{clientId}/competitors`. **Agency only**: the report, its
PDF and CSV, and the shared link never carry a suggestion.

A domain is a *probable rival* only if (a) it has the client's own restricted ending (`edu.au`
for `rmit.edu.au`; `ac.uk`, `gov.au`, `edu` and the other registry-restricted endings of the
14 markets for their clients; a client with none, a `.com`, has no probable rivals) AND (b) at
least one answer of the scan named a brand whose name matches its label ("Deakin University"
for `deakin.edu.au`). It is read from the client's newest finished scan that recorded the
fact; a scan from before it was recorded is passed over, and a client with no such scan has no
suggestions. A domain is suggested only if nobody holds it now: not the client's own domain or
confirmed sites, not an active rival of the list the next scan will use, nor that rival's
confirmed other sites. A rival the agency struck is suggested again.

Each suggestion is `domain`, `name` (to add it with: the label in capitals for two to four
letters, "UNSW", else capitalised, "Deakin"), `citations` (the scan's answered results citing
