**Errors:** `401`; `404` (another agency's client is the same `404` as an unknown one).
A client's scans, newest first.

post.description:
Queue a scan. Returns immediately; the work happens out of band.

**`202`, not `201`, and `ScanOut`, not `ScanDetailOut`** — Epic 9.5. This
used to run the whole pipeline inline, which Epic 9.2 measured at ~303s, and
Epic 9.3 found the real cost: the scan row sat in an uncommitted transaction
for that entire time, invisible to every other request. There was nothing
for a dashboard to poll because, as far as Postgres was concerned, the scan
did not exist yet.

The response model is `ScanOut` rather than `ScanDetailOut` with empty
fields. At `202` there is no prompt set and there are no results — the
prompt set is generated *by* the scan. Returning `ScanDetailOut` would
describe a shape this endpoint never has, and leave a caller unable to tell
"not generated yet" from "generated, and empty".

Poll `GET /scans/{scanId}` for completion; it carries the prompt set and
results once they exist.

Still costs real money once it runs — 20-30 prompts across every engine plus
a sentiment call per mention. `promptLimit` caps the set for verification.

Reuses the scan Epic 3's competitor detection created, if one is open, so a
detect-then-scan flow does not strand an empty scan.

**A scan already RUNNING is returned as it is, and no second executor is
started** — API key discipline audit, 2026-09-07. `executor.submit` used
to be unconditional, so re-running while a scan was in flight handed the
same row to a second executor, which re-paid for the chain up to a unique
violation. The executor now refuses a scan it cannot claim (see
`execute_scan`); this check simply declines to start a task that would be
refused. The `202` reports the scan in flight, which is what was asked for.

**`402 scan-limit-reached` since 2026-09-28** — `services/scan_allowance`.
One free scan per agency for life, forty a month on the plan; the gate is
on when billing is configured and off when it is not. The agency row is
locked before the count and the scan is inserted and committed under that
lock, so two requests at the cap cannot both take the last slot. A scan
already RUNNING is returned as before, and the open QUEUED scan a run
adopts is not counted against starting it.

**The free scan needs a Google sign-in since 2026-09-29.** A requesting
user with no linked Google identity, in a free agency, gets the 402 with
`SCAN_LIMIT_VERIFY_REQUIRED` — refused under the same lock, before the
count is consulted, and with no scan row created. Paid agencies and
exempt operators are unaffected.

Hide the getting-started checklist for this agency. **Auth required.**

**Per agency, and any seat holder may do it.** The checklist describes the
agency's account, so hiding it is an account-level choice, and it is not a
setting that changes what anyone can do — a member who dismisses it takes
nothing from the owner except a card the owner could also have closed.
That is why this is not behind `RequireAdmin`, unlike everything under
`/agencies/{id}`, which changes who holds a seat or who pays.

**Idempotent.** Dismissing twice is not an error and does not move the
timestamp: the first dismissal is the fact, and a second click on a stale
page is not a second decision.

**There is no un-dismiss.** The checklist is a first-week affordance; an
agency that closed it and wants it back has, by then, either done the
steps or decided not to. If that turns out to be wrong, clearing the
column is a one-line endpoint, not a design.

**Errors:** `401 authentication-required`.

get.description:
Liveness. Deliberately touches no dependency.

A liveness probe that checks the database causes an orchestrator to kill
and restart healthy API pods during a database blip, turning a partial
outage into a total one. Readiness is what should fail then.
Readiness. Verifies the datastores this service cannot serve without.

post.description:
A report, by share token. **No session required** — Epic 9.8.

This is the send path Epic 9's acceptance criterion needs: the prospect a
report is about has no account, and must not need one to read it.

**The token is the whole credential**, so the rules are narrow and worth
stating:

* **Read-only.** There is no sibling route that mutates anything by token.
  A holder cannot edit the competitor set, re-run the scan, or reach any
  other scan — the token resolves to exactly one row.
* **`404` for every rejection, with one code path.** An unknown, revoked or
  expired token, and one whose scan FAILED (3.29), is indistinguishable in
  both status and body. The only pre-check is the body's length bound (`422`
  for an empty or over-512 token); it says nothing about whether any token
  is real. Every plausible guess pays for the same index lookup.
* **The token is in the POST body, not the path**, so it stays out of
  request logs.
* **No `401`, ever.** A `401` would say "this token is real, authenticate to
  use it", which is precisely the bit an enumerator wants.
* **Same projection as the authenticated route.** `build_report` is reused
  rather than reimplemented, so the facts-only guarantee `test_facts_only.py`
  sweeps over this module covers this response too — a second assembly path
  would be a second place for a snippet to slip in. One field is blanked:
  `scanErrorCode`, which says why a scan is partial or failed and is for the
  agency alone (`build_public_report`).

**Errors:** `404` only.

A report PDF, by share token. **No session required** — Epic 9.14.

THE DECISION, STATED RATHER THAN DEFAULTED
------------------------------------------
A stranger holding a share token CAN download the PDF, and the share page
offers it. Three reasons, in order of weight:

1. **It exposes nothing new.** The PDF carries strictly the facts
   `POST /reports/shared` already serves to the same holder, rendered
   differently. Withholding it would not protect a single datum.
2. **The send path is the point.** Epic 9.8 built this token because "the
   prospect a report is about has no account, and must not need one to read
   it". Granting the harder-to-forward form (a live URL) while withholding
   the easy one (a file they can keep) is backwards for a mechanism whose
   whole job is *send*.
3. **A prospect wants a file.** The realistic next step for someone sent a
   report is forwarding it to a colleague or putting it in front of a
   budget holder, and a link that dies when they change jobs is worse for
   the agency than a PDF that does not.

**What it costs, said plainly: a downloaded PDF outlives revocation.**
Epic 9.14 accepted that cost when it was zero — links had no expiry and no
revocation, so the file took away nothing the link did not already give
away permanently — and marked this "the route to revisit when revocation
ships". Epic 9.21 shipped it, so this is that revisit, and the decision is
recorded rather than inherited.

**A revoked or expired link stops serving files immediately**, on the same
lookup as the JSON route: `scan_for_share_token` returns nothing and this
route 404s like any other miss. So does a link whose scan FAILED (3.29): the
token is kept for the agency to withdraw, but it opens nothing. What
revocation cannot do is recall a copy
already on someone's disk, and nothing can — the alternative would be
serving a watermarked or phone-home document, which is a different product
with different privacy properties. So the residual gap is real, bounded,
and named: revocation governs the LINK from the moment it is invoked, never
a file already downloaded.

Every rule the JSON share route states holds here unchanged, because it is
the same lookup: read-only, one code path, `404` for every rejection (the body's
token is bounded 1..512 by the schema, a `422` alike for real and fake
tokens, and no other shape check runs), and never a `401` — which would say "this token is real,
authenticate to use it".

**Errors:** `404` only.

get.description: A scan with its prompt set and every engine result.

The scan's technical audit, with every check in display order.

**A FAILED scan's audit carries no `technicalFoundation` and no `components`**
(3.30, extending 3.24), as on `POST`: `null` and `{}`, with `componentWeights` (this
audit's own weighting, with an unmeasured component's share redistributed) and every
fact about the site returned as before, the stored row not changed, and every other
status unchanged.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (unknown scan, another agency's, or not yet audited).

post.description:
Crawl the client's site and record structural signals plus per-check verdicts.

Makes **no model or search calls** — this is a page load plus two side
fetches (robots.txt, sitemap.xml). Cost is bandwidth and a few seconds.

Once an audit exists, re-scoring the scan includes Technical Foundation
instead of excluding it as `NOT_YET_MEASURED`.

One audit per scan, refreshed on re-run: a scan is a point-in-time claim
about a site, so a second audit of the same scan is a correction rather than
a new observation.

**A FAILED scan's audit carries no `technicalFoundation` and no `components`**
(3.30, extending 3.24): the sub-score is a score input and a failed scan shows no
score, and the component scores add up to it, so `technicalFoundation` is `null` and
`components` is `{}`. `componentWeights` (this audit's own weighting, with an
unmeasured component's share redistributed) and every fact about the site (the
checks, the signals) are returned as before, and the stored row keeps its values.
The agency check comes first, so another agency's failed scan is the same `404` as an
unknown one. The scan's status is read again after the crawl, so a scan that fails
while the audit runs is blanked too. Every other status is unchanged.

**One site read per agency at a time, and four at once** (2026-10-02), shared with
`POST /clients` and `POST /clients/{clientId}/reclassify`: while the agency's other
read is queued or running, or four agencies' reads are, this is a `429`. Checked
after the scan is found, so another agency's scan is still a `404`. A read that
waits more than a minute for the browser is refused with a `429` too, and the audit
already stored for the scan is kept. A scan's own audit, part of the scan, is not
one of these reads and is never refused: it waits up to two minutes for the
browser, and if the browser is not free by then the audit is recorded as `failed`
with `errorCode: BROWSER_BUSY` and the scan goes on.

**Errors:** `401`; `404` (unknown scan, or another agency's); `429 rate-limited`
(with `Retry-After: 60`).

get.description:
The scan's fix list as last generated, in rank order.

Returns an empty list with `status: "empty"` rather than 404 when nothing
has been generated yet: "no fixes yet" is a state of a scan that exists,
and the report renders its deterministic list in that case.

**A FAILED scan has no fixes served** (3.30, extending 3.24): the same `200` with
`status: "empty"` and `items: []` as a scan whose fixes were never generated,
whatever rows the scan kept. The generator's input includes a running scan's score
(founder's decision), so if the scan then fails nothing it wrote is served, on any
route. The rows are kept, not changed or deleted. Every other status is unchanged.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (unknown scan, or another agency's).

post.description:
Generate the scan's prioritised fix list.

Makes **one model call**. The candidates — which dimension gaps are worth a
line, which audit findings warrant a fix, and in what order — are decided
before the call by the same rules Epic 7 already applies on the client. The
model words them and judges priority and effort; it cannot add a
recommendation the measurement did not produce.

One row per candidate per scan, refreshed on re-run. A regenerated list is a
better statement of the same measurement, not a second measurement — but
`status` is the operator's, so it survives regeneration, and a candidate
that has been worked is kept even once it stops being measured.

A provider failure writes nothing and returns `status: "failed"` with a
reason code. The report still renders its deterministic fix list.

**A FAILED scan has no fixes served** (3.30, extending 3.24). For a scan still
running, the generator's input includes its score (founder's decision), and what it
writes can quote it. If the scan then fails, nothing it wrote is served, on any
route, and the rows are kept. So `POST` for a failed scan is `409`
`/problems/conflict`, "This scan failed, so no fixes are written for it.", with no
model call and no row written or changed. The agency check comes first, so another
agency's failed scan is the same `404` as an unknown one. A scan that fails while the
generation runs gets the same `409`: what the call wrote is kept, and not served.
Every other status is unchanged.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (unknown scan, or another agency's), `409` (failed scan).

get.description: The scan's generated prompt set.

Everything the narrative report needs, in one response.

**Presents; does not compute.** Score, competitors and audit are read from
the rows Epics 3-6 wrote. The only new numbers are aggregates — citation
counts per domain, mention shares, per-engine coverage — and each is a
count over stored facts.

Degraded data is reported, never smoothed over. `score` is null when the
scan was never scored, and a score with `status: "insufficient_data"` is a
different thing again: an unrunnable scan is never rendered as a low score.
`competitorSet` is null when detection never ran, and `audit` is null when
the site was never audited — in each case the report says so rather than
quietly omitting a beat.

**`csvExportAvailable`** says whether this report may offer "Download figures (CSV)"
(`GET /scans/{scanId}/report.csv`): the `REPORT_CSV_ENABLED` setting is on and this scan's
status is one the file is made for. It is set here and nowhere else, so it is false on the
PDF and on every public route; the web draws the link from it alone.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (unknown scan, or another agency's).

The report's figures as one CSV — F3, off unless `REPORT_CSV_ENABLED` is on.

**A rendering target, not a second report.** It calls the same `build_report` the JSON route
calls and writes what comes back (`services/report_csv.py`): no second query, no second
aggregation, and nothing the signed-in report does not already show. One long table, one
header row (`Section, Engine, Prompt, Item, Measure, Value`) and plain labels with their
units; the module says what each of its six sections holds (the first says whose scan it is,
its date, whether it is complete and its overall score) and what it leaves out.

**There is no token route, and there will not be one here.** A share link opens the report and
its PDF; it does not open this. The route is the agency's, scoped to the agency as the report
is, and `csvExportAvailable` is false on every public response.

**Off, it is not there.** With the setting off a signed-in caller gets a `404` with the body
an unknown path gets, whatever the scan, so it says nothing about the scan either. A signed-out
caller gets the `401` every signed-in route here gives.

**A scan with no figures to give is `409`** `/problems/scan-not-exportable`, with one plain
sentence: a FAILED scan (its score is withheld, as for sharing), a QUEUED or RUNNING one (its
figures are not final). The agency check runs first, so another agency's scan is a `404`
in every status and never a `409` that says how it ended. SUCCEEDED and PARTIAL are exported.

**Excel-safe:** a UTF-8 byte-order mark, and a leading apostrophe on any cell that begins
with `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, a tab, a carriage return or a full-width `＝＋－＠` (white space in
front does not hide it), and straight after a `;`, a tab or a line break inside a cell (each
starts a new cell or a new record in a spreadsheet), so a name somebody typed cannot become a
formula. The file is named `<client>-ai-visibility-<date>.csv`, the client reduced as the
PDF's name is.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (off, or unknown scan, or another agency's), `409` (no figures yet).

The same report, as a PDF — Epic 9.14 (Epic 9 send path, slice 3).

**A rendering target, not a second report.** It calls the same
`build_report` the JSON route calls and renders what comes back; there is no
second query, no second aggregation and no second set of numbers. A PDF
assembled independently would eventually disagree with the page it was
downloaded from, and the disagreement would reach a client.

It degrades exactly as the web report does, because it is derived from the
same payload: a null composite prints "Not scored" and never a zero,
`insufficient_data` gets its own sentence, an excluded dimension prints its
reason rather than a sub-score, a null competitor set says detection did not
run instead of quietly dropping the beat, and an empty `actionItems` renders
the deterministic fix derivation — the case api-contracts.md's note on that
field describes.

**No dependency was added to build this.** WeasyPrint's required `Pyphen` is
GPL/LGPL/MPL, which the dependency-licensing rule blocks; React-PDF is a Node library and
this is a Python process. See `services/pdf.py` for the full assessment.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (unknown scan, or another agency's).

Cursor-paginated engine results.

Separate from the scan detail because a full scan is 20-30 prompts times
every engine — 60+ rows with nested mentions and citations, which is a lot
to return in one body once a third engine is added.

The most recent stored Score for a scan, with the competitor comparison.

The comparison and the subject's average position are derived from
persisted rows on read rather than stored — they are a pure function of data
already in the database, and a second copy could fall out of step with the
first. Reading a score computes no score and writes nothing.

**A FAILED scan has no score** (3.30, extending 3.24): the same `404` as a scan
not yet scored, with the detail "This scan failed, so it has no score.",
whatever rows the scan kept. They are not read, changed or deleted.

**Errors:** `401`; `404` (unknown scan, another agency's, not yet scored, or
failed).

post.description:
Compute and store the AI Visibility Score for a scan.

**Makes no provider calls and costs nothing** — scoring is pure arithmetic
over rows Epic 4 already persisted. Sentiment is read from storage, never
re-classified (scoring-spec.md rule 4), which is what makes re-scoring
reproducible.

**Re-scoring INSERTS a new row** rather than overwriting. A Score is a dated
claim under a named `formulaVersion`; overwriting would erase the history
before/after reporting depends on.

**A FAILED scan is not scored** (3.30, extending 3.24): `409`
`/problems/conflict`, and no Score row is written or refreshed. A failed scan
has no score that is ever shown, and the rows it kept from before it failed
are neither changed nor deleted. The agency check comes first, so another
agency's failed scan is the same `404` as an unknown one. The status is read
under a row lock held until the score is committed, so a scan that fails
while this runs either fails first (`409`) or is scored first and fails
after. Every other status is scored as before.

**A scan matched under an earlier rule is not re-scored** (3.97): `409`
`/problems/conflict`, and no Score row is written or refreshed. Formula `v7`
changed how a brand is matched, not only the arithmetic, and answer text is
never stored, so a scan whose matches were made before v7 cannot be matched
again. Scoring it here would read those stored matches and write a row labelled
`v7` from matches v7 did not make. What matched a scan is recorded on it,
stamped when its run starts and read as `pre-v7` where nothing recorded it, and
any scan not matched by the current rule is refused with a detail that says to
run a new scan. The agency check and the failed-scan check come first, so
another agency's scan is the same `404` as an unknown one and a failed scan
keeps its own `409`. The rows the scan already has are neither changed nor
deleted. A scan's own run still scores it at the end.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (unknown scan, or another agency's), `409` (failed
scan, or a scan matched under an earlier rule).

**A FAILED scan lists none** (3.30, extending 3.24): `[]`, the same `200` as a
scan not yet scored, whatever rows the scan kept. They are not read, changed

delete.description:
Take the public link down — Epic 9.21. The inverse of the POST above.

**`DELETE` on the same path the mint uses**, because the thing being
removed is the resource that path names. The alternative shapes — a
`POST .../share/revoke`, or a `PATCH` with a null token — either invent a
second noun for one capability or make "unshare" reachable from an endpoint
whose job is to describe a scan.

**`204`, and idempotent.** Revoking a scan that was never shared is not an
error: the caller asked for it not to be readable, and it is not. Answering
`404` there would report on something they did not ask about, and `409`
would invite a retry loop over a state that is already correct. Nothing is
returned because there is nothing left to describe.

**After this, the token is gone for both read routes**, JSON and PDF, on
the same code path as a token that never existed — `scan_for_share_token`
is where the rule lives, so neither route can drift into treating a revoked
link as its own kind of wrong. A stranger holding the old URL gets exactly
the 404 an enumerator gets.

**What it does not reach: a PDF already downloaded.** Nothing can. The link
stops serving; a file on someone's disk is theirs. Said here and on the PDF
route rather than left for a reader to wonder about.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (unknown scan, or another agency's).

post.description:
Mint (or return) the public link for this scan's report — Epic 9.8.

**An explicit action, not a side effect of running a scan.** A scan is a
private measurement until an agency decides otherwise; publishing every
report at creation time and relying on the URL being unknown would make
that decision for them. This is the moment they make it.

**`200`, not `201`, and idempotent.** While the scan has a live link,
calling again returns that link exactly as it is: the same token and the
same `expiresAt`, with nothing written. Every extra token would be a URL
nobody is tracking, so the second call mints nothing and does not claim
to.

**A press on a live link does not move its end** — Epic 9.21, as changed by
checklist 3.28 (the founder's decision). The share bar says links last 30
days from when they are created, and "The link works until ..." names the
end the link was given, so both stay true of the link already sent. Only
when no link is live does a press make one: a scan never shared, a
withdrawn link, or one that has ended. That is a NEW token with a fresh 30
days. An ended token is replaced, not revived, so the address that stopped
working stays dead on both public routes. `services/share.py` carries the
argument in full.

**A FAILED scan cannot be shared** (3.24): `409`
`/problems/failed-scan-not-shareable`. Its score is never shown, so there
is no report to send. PARTIAL and every other status are unchanged. The
status is read again under the row lock, so a scan that fails while this
request is in flight is refused the same way and nothing is written. A link
minted before the scan failed stays on the row, so it can still be
withdrawn, but it no longer opens the report (3.29): the public routes
refuse it like a withdrawn one.

**Errors:** `401`, `404` (unknown scan, or another agency's), `409`
(failed scan).

delete.description:
Remove a seat. **Every session that seat holds dies immediately.**

Not merely the seat. `sessions.py` opens by saying this is why the product
has a server-side session store at all rather than JWTs: "when an agency
removes a seat, that person's access has to end *now* — not whenever their
access token happens to expire". This endpoint is the case that argument was
made for, so it calls `revoke_all_for_user` rather than relying on the
fallback.

There IS a fallback, and it is not the mechanism: `deps.current_principal`
re-reads the user on every request and 401s on a soft-deleted row, so access
would end on the removed user's next call even if revocation were skipped.
That closes the door within one request. Revocation closes it within zero,
and the difference is a request that is already in flight.

The row is soft-deleted, so the seat is released while `scans.requested_by_
user_id` and the rest of that person's history stay intact — the rule
`models/base.py` states for the whole schema.

**Two refusals, both `409`:**

* Removing yourself. An owner who deletes their own row is authenticated by
  a session that is about to be revoked, mid-request. `logout-all` is the
  deliberate version of signing yourself out.
* Removing the last active owner. `UserRole` says why in the model: an
  agency with no owner has nobody who can manage seats — including nobody
  who can undo this.

**Errors:** `401`, `403`, `404` (unknown user, or another agency's — never
`403`, which would confirm the id), `409`.
